analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to order food recalls when products are believed contaminated and dangerous.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to order companies to stop distributing any food believed to be adulterated and dangerous to human health, and to order a full recall after a quick informal hearing [S2][S3]. At the time, the FDA could only ask food companies to recall contaminated products voluntarily; companies could refuse. This bill would have made compliance mandatory, with penalties for refusal [S2][S3]. It was introduced in late September 2002, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never advanced [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would be protected from contaminated food more quickly. Under the voluntary system, a company that disagreed with the FDA about whether its product was dangerous could keep selling it while the agency negotiated. Mandatory orders with a recall timetable and progress reports would have taken contaminated products off shelves faster [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the government to order an immediate halt to distribution of any food it has a reasonable basis to believe is adulterated and a risk to human health — covering manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers [S2][S3].

After an informal hearing held within 10 days, the Secretary could convert the stop-distribution order into a full recall, with a set timetable and periodic progress reports, and refusing to comply would become a prohibited act under the food and drug law [S2][S3].
Special recall rules for infant formula would apply, directing the Secretary to use the existing infant formula recall provisions instead of the new general ones [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, who would bear the cost of halting sales and carrying out mandated recalls when the government found a reasonable basis to believe their products were dangerous, and who would face legal penalties for refusing [S2][S3]. Companies that believed they were wrongly targeted would get an informal hearing within 10 days and could have the order vacated if the evidence was insufficient [S2].

drawbacks.text: A company could be forced to stop distributing its product — and later recall it — on a 'reasonable basis' standard short of proof, and while it would get a hearing within 10 days, the order takes effect first and costs accrue immediately [S2][S3].

Recalls are expensive: pulling product from shelves, notifying customers, and destroying inventory fall on the company even when the suspicion turns out to be wrong, and those costs can be passed to consumers through prices. The bill sets no process for compensating companies whose orders are later vacated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster removal of dangerous food from store shelves, including deadly risks like contaminated meat, produce, and infant formula. The cost falls on food companies, which may have to halt sales and recall product on a reasonable-belief standard before the evidence is complete — though the 10-day hearing and the power to vacate insufficiently supported orders give them a check [S2][S3]. For most consumers, quicker recalls are worth far more than the compliance costs, which is why mandatory recall authority eventually became law in a later Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, which never held a hearing or voted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on September 26, 2002, near the end of the 107th Congress, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which on October 8, 2002 sent it to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill died in subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers came out ahead: they kept the voluntary recall system in which the FDA could ask but not order a recall, and faced no penalty for refusing. Consumers gained nothing from this bill's death, though stronger mandatory recall authority for the FDA was enacted in a later Congress.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give the FDA mandatory food recall authority.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 107th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup before Congress ended.

against.name: Food industry
against.role: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers subject to the proposed recall orders
against.what_they_did: The food industry had long opposed granting the FDA mandatory recall authority, preferring the voluntary system, and continued to resist it for years afterward.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show the split; it had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would force them to halt distribution and recall food on a government order — with penalties for refusing — instead of recalling voluntarily. Their interest in keeping the voluntary system ran against faster protection for consumers eating possibly contaminated food.
